title: Wishing You a Regret-Free Winter Break
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: In his last article of 2024, Stuart reflects on Bronnie Ware's The Top Five Regrets of the Dying as a lens for how to spend winter break intentionally rather than just going through the motions. He walks through each of Ware's five deathbed regrets -- living authentically, working too hard, not expressing feelings, losing touch with friends, and not choosing happiness -- and attaches a concrete personal intention to each one, from limiting work to three or four days off to deliberately reconnecting with old friends from his Baltimore years. He connects the "happiness is a choice" regret to his own choice to pause drinking a year earlier, framing it as a small but real example of intentional living. The piece functions as both a personal essay and an implicit invitation for readers to use their own break similarly, treating rest as something to be practiced rather than passively received.
points: Stuart reframes winter break planning around Bronnie Ware's five deathbed regrets rather than typical rest-and-recharge advice, giving the reflection more weight and specificity.
His self-imposed rule of capping work during break to "three or four" of seventeen days operationalizes "I wish I hadn't worked so hard" into something trackable.
He explicitly extends MGCs (Moments of Genuine Connection), a classroom practice, into his personal life as a way to "express my feelings" outside of school.
The reference to voluntarily pausing alcohol a year prior is offered as concrete evidence that small, deliberate choices can shift overall happiness, not just abstract sentiment.
quotes: As we go into break, I'm thinking about this idea of living with no regrets. As a middle-aged guy, it can be easy to go through the motions. This is what most folks do. The trouble is, going through the motions leads to regrets over time.

I wish I hadn't worked so hard. I've got 17 days off of school once this Friday hits. I'll give myself three or four of those days to do work. Any work-related thoughts that intrude on the other 13-14 days, I'll write them in my journal and keep on with my life.

I wish I had the courage to express my feelings. For me this break, I want to focus on expressing feelings that are helpful, positive, true. Think of it as MGCs but outside the classroom and from my heart to someone else's.

This is probably the most convicting regret from Ware's whole book — at least for me. I'm bad at staying in touch with folks. But Crystal and I decided to use a few days before New Years to visit with old friends from our Baltimore days.

It was a choice to pause my drinking just over a year ago, and it's a choice that's led to a surprising increase in my overall happiness. Tiny example. But for this break, how could I choose to laugh more?
